patient.chief_complaint: Progressive confusion and personality change over 1 week in HCC patient on sorafenib
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T. is a 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma receiving sorafenib, presenting with a 1-week history of progressive confusion, word-finding difficulty, and behavioral change. His wife described increasing irritability, repeated conversations, and inability to balance his finances — activities he normally handles. He denies hematemesis or melena. He reports worsening nausea and diarrhea over the prior 3 weeks that his oncologist attributed to sorafenib side effects (sorafenib commonly causes diarrhea and nausea). His sorafenib dose has not been adjusted despite the diarrhea, which has been 3-5 watery stools per day. He has low-grade fever 38.2°C on admission. The moderate-difficulty features in this case include: (1) sorafenib as potential direct neurotoxin (sorafenib-associated encephalopathy is rare but recognized), (2) sorafenib-induced diarrhea causing electrolyte disturbance as HE precipitant (hypokalemia), (3) concurrent low-grade fever requiring SBP exclusion, and (4) the need to distinguish HE from sorafenib-related CNS toxicity. The key diagnostic finding will be ammonia elevation with supporting EEG changes and SBP exclusion.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II-III), alcoholic cirrhosis with HCC on sorafenib (Child-Pugh B, MELD 16) — precipitated by sorafenib-induced diarrhea causing hypokalemia (K 2.8), hypomagnesemia, dehydration, and pre-renal AKI; concurrent low-grade fever requires SBP exclusion.

differential.key_features: Rare but reported sorafenib encephalopathy; would not produce asterixis or rapid lactulose response.
HCC rarely metastasizes to brain; would expect focal deficits and consider MRI if course atypical.
AKI is mostly pre-renal from diarrhea-related volume loss; reassess after fluid resuscitation.
Dehydration is a precipitant of HE in this patient, not a sole cause given cirrhosis and ammonia elevation.

optimal_actions.action: Comprehensive labs: CMP including AST/ALT/bilirubin/INR/albumin, ammonia, CBC, glucose, electrolytes (Na, K, Mg), BUN/Cr, lactate, blood cultures and urine cultures; toxicology if substance use plausible. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: K 2.8, Mg low, Cr elevated (AKI), ammonia elevated; identify volume status and precipitants.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.

Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (AASLD/EASL HE management; sorafenib adverse effects in cirrhosis; diarrhea-induced electrolyte HE).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering sorafenib (consider dose reduction), lactulose, rifaximin, loperamide if used (caution); review hepatic dosing; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: Diagnostic paracentesis given low-grade fever and ascites to exclude SBP.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ascitic PMN count to confirm or exclude SBP.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — consider if no improvement with electrolyte/volume correction. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
Consult hepatology and oncology — discuss sorafenib continuation vs hold — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Aggressive IV potassium and magnesium repletion (cardiac monitoring during K repletion).
Volume resuscitation with albumin to reverse pre-renal AKI.
Lactulose titrated to 2-4 soft stools/day; rifaximin 550 mg BID.
Discuss sorafenib hold vs dose-reduction with oncology pending HE resolution.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not give loperamide aggressively in cirrhosis (constipation precipitates HE) — manage diarrhea via sorafenib dose adjustment instead.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Targeted therapies (sorafenib) commonly cause diarrhea; the electrolyte/volume consequences are a frequent HE precipitant in HCC patients on these drugs.
Fever in a cirrhotic with ascites is SBP until proven otherwise — paracentesis mandatory.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute encephalopathy to HCC progression or 'sorafenib brain toxicity' and order extensive oncologic imaging.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The sorafenib-related issue here is diarrhea → electrolyte loss → HE; direct CNS toxicity is rare.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Default to broad-spectrum antibiotics without source workup.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mandatory paracentesis to exclude SBP; targeted empiric therapy only when ascitic PMN ≥250 or strong other source.
